question_text: If x + y = 3 is the equation of the chord AB of the circle x² + y² − 2x + 4y − 8 = 0, find the equation of the circle having AB as diameter.

insider_note: The centre of S + λL = 0 always has a MINUS sign on the y-coordinate half of it — write the centre as ((2 − λ)/2, −(4 + λ)/2) explicitly rather than trusting a half-remembered shortcut, or the diameter condition solves to the wrong λ.
formula_note: S + λL = 0 is the family of every circle through the two points where the circle S meets the line L — the same one-parameter idea as S + λS′ = 0 for two circles, but built from a circle and a line instead. A chord becomes a diameter exactly when the family's own centre lies on L; that condition is what fixes λ here.

steps.label: Write the family through S and L
steps.margin_note: First mark. Every circle through the same two points as S and the line L can be written this way.
lines: Any circle through the points of intersection
of S = 0 and L = 0 is S + λL = 0
(At a point on both, S = 0 and L = 0, so

lines.text: S + λL = 0 there, for every number λ.)

lines: S + λL = x² + y² − 2x + 4y − 8 + λ(x + y − 3)
steps.why: S + λL = 0 is a one-parameter family of circles that all pass through the SAME two points where the line L cuts the circle S — choosing the right λ picks out one member of this family.
common_mistakes: Switching between S + λL = 0 and S − λL = 0 part way through. Both give the same circles, but λ changes sign (S − λL = 0 gives λ = 4), so keep one form from start to finish.
Losing the constant −8 while collecting terms with λ.
steps.memory_tip: S + λL = 0 is the standard family formula whenever a circle must pass through the same two points as another circle and a line.

steps.label: Write the centre of the family
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Read the centre straight from the coefficients in step 1 — half of each, then negate.

lines.text: The centre of a circle is (−g, −f):

lines: Centre of the above circle is
steps.why: For a circle x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 the centre is (−g, −f) — halving the x and y coefficients from step 1 and negating gives this centre in terms of λ.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the negative sign on the y-coordinate, which then breaks the diameter condition in the next step.
Halving the coefficients but skipping the negation.
steps.memory_tip: Centre = −(half the x-coefficient), −(half the y-coefficient) — always two negatives, one for each coordinate.

steps.label: Apply the diameter condition
steps.margin_note: Last two marks: one for finding λ, one for the final circle. The line L becomes a diameter exactly when the centre lies on L.

lines.text: AB lies on L. A chord is a diameter exactly
when it passes through the centre.

lines: Line L = 0 becomes a diameter if the
centre lies on L ≡ x + y − 3 = 0

lines.text: Check: its centre (3, 0) lies on x + y = 3.

steps.why: A chord is a diameter of a circle exactly when the circle's centre lies on it — substituting the family's centre into L = 0 pins down the one member of the family whose diameter is AB.
common_mistakes: Substituting the centre into S = 0 instead of L = 0.
Sign error from the missing minus on the y-coordinate, giving a wrong λ and a wrong final circle.
steps.memory_tip: Diameter condition = centre on the line, always — the same test works for any 'AB is a diameter' question, whatever the numbers.
lines_compact: Line L = 0 becomes a diameter if the
centre lies on L ≡ x + y − 3 = 0
